slides.headline: September 29, 1997: India launched its own rocket, carrying its own satellite, for the first time.
PSLV-C1 lifted off from Sriharikota on September 29, 1997, carrying the IRS-1D satellite
slides.body: It was the first operational flight of the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle - India's own launch vehicle, developed without relying on another country for its critical stages. A helium leak left IRS-1D in a lower, elliptical orbit than planned, not the intended outcome, but the satellite reached space under Indian power.

slides.headline: A satellite that should have struggled kept working for over 12 years.
slides.body: IRS-1D, India's fourth Indian Remote Sensing satellite, was designed for a shorter mission but stayed operational until January 2010 - more than a decade past its design life - carrying imaging payloads that became a mainstay of India's earth observation capability. PSLV itself went on to become one of the most reliable launch vehicles in the world.

slides.eyebrow: Why it matters for Viksit Bharat 2047
slides.headline: A rocket that didn't go perfectly still built the foundation for everything that came after.
slides.body: A Viksit Bharat by 2047 needs the ability to put its own hardware into space on its own terms. PSLV-C1's imperfect first flight is exactly where that ability started - and PSLV has since launched satellites for dozens of countries.
